observations.question: How can I tell whether I really understand a business, rather than just know its products?

completion.answer:
You can tell you really understand a business when you can confidently predict its future cash flows and competitive position over many years, and when you know exactly where your knowledge ends. If you have any doubt about whether something is inside your circle of competence, it isn’t. That is the first and most reliable test.

### The “doubt” test

Warren Buffett gave a blunt rule at the 2002 meeting: “if you have doubts about something being into your circle of competence, it isn’t.” [1] He added that it is better to be well within the circle than to tiptoe along the line. [1] This means that genuine understanding produces a feeling of certainty, not a vague sense that you “sort of” get it. If you find yourself rationalising or hoping, you probably only know the product, not the business.

### The predictability test

Understanding a business means being able to forecast its economics with high confidence. In the 1992 letter, Buffett wrote that Berkshire sticks to businesses that are “relatively simple and stable in character. If a business is complex or subject to constant change, we’re not smart enough to predict future cash flows.” [2] He and Charlie Munger look for operations “virtually certain to possess enormous competitive strength ten or twenty years from now.” [4] They call such companies “The Inevitables” – firms like Coca‑Cola and Gillette whose dominance is not seriously questioned by any sensible observer. [4] If you cannot describe why the business will still be strong a decade from now, you do not understand it; you only know its current products.

### The valuation test

Knowing products does not equal knowing how to value the enterprise. At the 1998 meeting, Buffett explained that they treat risk as a go/no‑go valve: if they cannot see the future clearly, they simply give up rather than adjust a discount rate. [3] The value of any business is determined by the cash inflows and outflows expected during its remaining life, discounted at an appropriate interest rate. [2] If you cannot estimate those future “coupons” – the cash the business will generate – you lack the understanding needed to invest. Buffett noted that you can understand a company like General Motors “in a general way” but still not be able to value it. [1] That distinction is crucial: product knowledge is general; valuation requires a specific, reasoned estimate of future economics.

### The boundary test

A hallmark of real competence is knowing where it ends. At the 2014 meeting, Buffett admitted he went outside his circle in retail and when he bought control of Berkshire Hathaway. [5] He said being realistic about your own talents and shortcomings is essential, and that some people are much better at it than others. [5] Munger added that if you have competence, you “almost automatically have a feeling of where the edge of the competence is.” [1] He gave a simple analogy: if you are five‑foot‑two, you know you have no future in the NBA. [5] Similarly, if you cannot articulate why a business will succeed and where your knowledge stops, you are probably outside your circle.

### A concrete example

Buffett contrasted two cases at the 2002 meeting. He said he could evaluate a business like Larson‑Juhl (a picture‑framing company) immediately because it was within his circle. But when he was offered a large finance company, he understood every individual transaction yet did not regard the whole enterprise as within his competence. [1] That shows the difference: understanding transactions is not the same as understanding the business’s durability, funding needs, and competitive dynamics menus. If you can only list products or describe operations but cannot assess long‑term competitive advantage and cash‑flow predictability, you do not truly understand the business.

observations.question: What makes reported profit different from cash an owner can actually take out of a business?

completion.answer:
Reported profit (GAAP net income) differs from the cash an owner can actually take out because GAAP earnings include non‑cash charges but **do not deduct the capital spending required to keep the business competitive**. The correct measure for an owner is “owner earnings,” which adjusts reported profit for both of these factors.

### 1. Non‑cash charges are added back
Depreciation, amortization, depletion, and certain other non‑cash items (such as purchase‑price inventory write‑offs and deferred‑tax adjustments) reduce reported earnings but do not consume cash. In the owner‑earnings formula these are added back to reported earnings [1]. For example, in the Scott Fetzer illustration, the “new” company (N) reported $28.6 million of net income while the “old” company (O) reported $40.2 million – yet both generated identical cash because the extra $11.6 million of charges in column N were purely accounting entries [1].

### 2. Maintenance capital expenditures must be subtracted
The critical subtraction is the **average annual amount of capitalized expenditures for plant and equipment that the business requires to fully maintain its long‑term competitive position and its unit volume** [1]. If the business also needs additional working capital to hold its ground, that increment is subtracted as well [1]. GAAP earnings never deduct this maintenance‑capex figure; they only deduct historical depreciation, which is often lower than the real cash needed to stay in place. As Buffett notes, “Most managers probably will acknowledge that they need to spend something more than (b) [depreciation] on their businesses over the longer term just to hold their ground” [1]. When maintenance capex exceeds depreciation, GAAP earnings overstate owner earnings – a common situation in manufacturing, retailing, extractive industries, and utilities [1].

### 3. The owner‑earnings formula
The full definition from the 1986 letter is:

> Owner earnings = (a) reported earnings  
> + (b) depreciation, depletion, amortization, and certain other non‑cash charges  
> – (c) the average annual amount of capitalized expenditures for plant and equipment, etc. that the business requires to fully maintain its long‑term competitive position and its unit volume (plus any additional working capital needed to maintain that position) [1].

This formula makes clear that the cash an owner can actually withdraw is **reported profit adjusted for non‑cash items and then reduced by the necessary reinvestment to keep the business healthy**. The result is often far from GAAP net income. For Scott Fetzer, Buffett and Munger believed that (c) was “very close to the ‘old’ company’s (b) number of $8.3 million,” so owner earnings were much better depicted by the O‑column earnings of $40.2 million than by the N‑column GAAP figure of $28.6 million [1].

### 4. Why EBITDA is misleading
A common but dangerous shortcut is EBITDA (earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization). EBITDA adds back all non‑cash charges but **ignores the subtraction of maintenance capex**. Buffett calls it “utter nonsense” because “any business with significant fixed assets almost always has with it a concomitant requirement that major cash be reinvested in order simply to stay in the same place” [3]. Using EBITDA to measure an owner’s distributable cash is like claiming a company never needs to replace its plant – a fantasy that has been used to justify overpriced securities [1][3].

### 5. The “Frozen Corporation” thought experiment
Ben Graham’s “Frozen Corporation” – a company whose charter forbids ever paying cash to owners – is worth nothing, because “a financial asset has to give you back cash to justify you laying out cash for it now” [3]. This illustrates that the only cash that matters to an owner is what can eventually be taken out, after all necessary reinvestment. Reported profit that never turns into distributable cash is irrelevant.

### Summary
Reported profit differs from cash an owner can take out because:
- It includes non‑cash charges that must be added back.
- It does **not** subtract the capital spending needed to maintain the business’s competitive position (maintenance capex and any required working‑capital increases).
- The correct metric is owner earnings, which makes both adjustments. For many businesses, maintenance capex exceeds depreciation, so GAAP earnings overstate true distributable cash. For a few businesses (e.g., a bridge or a long‑lived gas field), maintenance capex is tiny, and EBITDA may be a reasonable shorthand – but for most enterprises it is dangerously misleading [1][3].

observations.question: how to evaluate a stock

completion.answer:
To evaluate a stock using the framework from the Berkshire archive, you must determine the intrinsic value of the underlying business and buy only when the market price offers a clear margin of safety. This is not a mechanical formula but a disciplined, business-like process that combines qualitative judgment with a quantitative estimate of future cash flows.

### 1. Define Your Circle of Competence
The first step is to determine if the business lies within your “circle of competence” [2:u0114]. Buffett states that he and Munger “try to stick to businesses we believe we understand. That means they must be relatively simple and stable in character. If a business is complex or subject to constant change, we’re not smart enough to predict future cash flows” [1:u0084]. If you cannot make a reasonable estimate of future earnings, “just forget it and move on” [3:p0013]. You do not need to be an expert on every company, but you must know the boundaries of your own knowledge [2:u0114].

### 2. Assess the Quality and Durability of the Business
Next, evaluate the business’s competitive position. The ideal business is one that is “unlikely to experience major change” and possesses “enormous competitive strength ten or twenty years from now” [2:u0101]. Buffett calls these “The Inevitables”—companies like Coca-Cola and Gillette that dominate their fields and are virtually certain to continue doing so for an investment lifetime [2:u0107].

The best business to own is one that “over an extended period can employ large amounts of incremental capital at very high rates of return” [1:u0083]. Growth is not automatically good; “growth benefits investors only when the business in point can invest at incremental returns that are enticing—in other words, only when each dollar used to finance the growth creates over a dollar of long-term market value” [1:u0080]. Management must also be “honest and competent” [1:u0074].

### 3. Estimate Future Cash Flows (The “Coupons”)
The core of the valuation is estimating the future cash flows the business will generate. Buffett defines intrinsic value as “the discounted value of the cash that can be taken out of a business during its remaining life” [4:u0023]. The formula is the same for stocks as for bonds, but unlike a bond, the equity “coupons” must be estimated by the analyst [1:u0081].

This requires answering Aesop’s three questions: “How certain are you that there are indeed birds in the bush? When will they emerge and how many will there be? What is the risk-free interest rate (which we consider to be the yield on long-term U.S. bonds)?” [5:p12-4]. Because precise numbers are foolish, “working with a range of possibilities is the better approach” [5:p12-7]. If the range is so wide that no useful conclusion can be reached, the stock should be passed over [5:p12-8].

### 4. Discount to Present Value and Apply a Margin of Safety
Once you have a range of estimated future cash flows, you discount them back to the present using the risk-free interest rate [1:u0081], [5:p12-4]. This gives you a range for the intrinsic value of the business.

Finally, compare the current market price to your calculated intrinsic value range. “If we calculate the value of a common stock to be only slightly higher than its price, we’re not interested in buying” [1:u0085]. You must insist on a “margin of safety” in the purchase price, which Buffett calls “the cornerstone of investment success” [1:u0085]. Even the best business can be a bad investment if you overpay: “You can, of course, pay too much for even the best of businesses” [2:u0110].

### 5. Adopt the Right Temperament
Throughout this process, the investor must ignore macro predictions and market noise. “Forming macro opinions or listening to the macro or market predictions of others is a waste of time” [3:p0016]. “Focus on the future productivity of the asset you are considering” [3:p0013]. View market volatility as a friend, not a foe; “a climate of fear is your friend when investing; a euphoric world is your enemy” [3:p0022].

The recommended holding period is long: “If you aren’t willing to own a stock for ten years, don’t even think about owning it for ten minutes” [2:u0116]. For those who cannot or will not do this work, the archive recommends a low-cost S&P 500 index fund as the superior alternative [2:u0113], [3:p0028].

observations.question: How would I work out what a company is worth before deciding whether its shares are a bargain?

completion.answer:
To work out what a company is worth before deciding whether its shares are a bargain, you must estimate its **intrinsic value** – the discounted value of all the cash that can be taken out of the business during its remaining life – and then compare that figure to the current market price. The process is straightforward in concept but requires discipline, self-awareness, and a willingness to accept uncertainty. The key steps, drawn from Warren Buffett’s own explanations, are:

1. **Stay inside your circle of competence.**  
2. **Estimate future distributable cash flows (owner earnings).**  
3. **Discount those flows at a reasonable interest rate.**  
4. **Compare the resulting intrinsic value per share to the stock price.**

---

### 1. Know what you understand – and what you don’t

Before you can value a company, you must be confident that you understand its business well enough to make a rough estimate of its future earnings. Buffett puts it bluntly: “If you have doubts about something being into your circle of competence, it isn’t” [1]. You do not need to be an expert in every industry, but you must be able to answer basic questions: How does the company earn money? What are its competitive advantages? What are the normal economics of the business? If you cannot make a “rough estimate of the asset’s future earnings, just forget it and move on” [4].

Even Buffett admits he has sometimes strayed outside his circle – for example, in retail and in his original purchase of Berkshire itself [5]. The ability to recognize the boundary is itself a skill. Charlie Munger adds that “if you have competence, you almost automatically have a feeling of where the edge of the competence is” [1]. If you are unsure, you are probably outside it.

---

### 2. Estimate future distributable cash flows

Intrinsic value is not about reported earnings or book value. Buffett defines it as “the discounted value of the cash that can be taken out of a business during its remaining life” [3]. For a company you might own outright, that means the cash you could actually withdraw after maintaining the business. For a stock, it means your proportionate share of those future cash flows.

In practice, you start with **owner earnings** – a concept that adjusts reported earnings for maintenance capital expenditure and certain non-cash charges. In the 2004 annual meeting, Buffett endorsed an audience member’s approach that used “look-through earnings” (Berkshire’s share of earnings from both controlled and partially owned businesses) as a proxy for distributable cash, while noting that capital expenditure typically exceeds depreciation over time [2]. The key is to focus on the cash the business can generate for owners, not on accounting numbers.

Buffett’s own examples illustrate the method. When he bought a Nebraska farm in 1986, he calculated the “normalized return” from the farm to be about 10% based on expected crop yields and operating expenses [4]. For a New York retail property, he estimated the “unleveraged current yield” at about 10% and then considered how income would grow as below-market leases expired [4]. In both cases, he thought only about what the asset would produce, not about daily price changes.

For a stock, you need to estimate an earnings range for five years out or more. “If the answer is yes, we will buy the stock (or business) if it sells at a reasonable price in relation to the bottom boundary of our estimate” [4]. If you cannot make that estimate, move on.

---

### 3. Discount the cash flows at an appropriate rate

Once you have a stream of estimated future cash flows, you discount them back to the present to arrive at a single intrinsic value. The discount rate should reflect the long-term risk-free rate (e.g., the yield on long-term government bonds) plus a risk premium appropriate for the business. In the 2004 meeting, Buffett did not quarrel with the audience member’s use of a 7% discount rate, but he stressed that “the question of what number to use” is subjective and that “neither one of us knows” the right variables [2].

The calculation typically includes a terminal value – the value of cash flows beyond the explicit forecast period. The audience member assumed the business would stop growing after 20 years and then produce a perpetual 7% coupon, which Buffett accepted as a reasonable framework [2]. The exact numbers are less important than the logic: “the business today is worth the present value of all the cash it can distribute between now and Judgment Day” [2].

---

### 4. Compare intrinsic value to the market price

If your estimated intrinsic value per share is significantly above the current stock price, the shares may be a bargain. Buffett emphasizes that you should focus on the “bottom boundary” of your estimate – a conservative figure – and buy only when the price is well below that [4]. This provides a margin of safety.

Crucially, you must ignore short-term market noise. “Games are won by players who focus on the playing field – not by those whose eyes are glued to the scoreboard” [4]. A stock’s daily price fluctuations are like a moody neighbor shouting offers for your farm; you can use them to your advantage only if you have already done your homework [4].

---

### A note on uncertainty

Intrinsic value is always a “highly subjective figure that will change both as estimates of future cash flows are revised and as interest rates move” [3]. No one can pinpoint it exactly. The goal is not precision but a reasonable range. If you cannot estimate that range with confidence, you are not ready to buy. As Buffett says, “omniscience isn’t necessary; you only need to understand the actions you undertake” [4].

For most non-professional investors, the simplest path is to own a low-cost S&P 500 index fund, which automatically provides diversification and avoids the need to value individual companies [4]. But if you choose to value a specific business, the method above – rooted in understanding, cash-flow estimation, and discounting – is the only logical way to decide whether its shares are a bargain.

observations.question: How can I tell whether I really understand a business, rather than just know its products?

completion.answer:
## The core test: doubt itself is the answer

If you have any doubt about whether a business is inside your circle of competence, it isn't. As Buffett put it in 2002: "if you have doubts about something being into your circle of competence, it isn't." [1] That is the single most practical diagnostic. Product familiarity is not the same as business understanding, and the difference shows up precisely where doubt appears.

## Knowing the product vs. knowing the economics

Understanding a product means you can describe what a company sells, how it works, and perhaps why customers buy it. Understanding a business means you can evaluate its long-term economics: the durability of its competitive advantage, the likely range of future cash flows, and whether those cash flows can be predicted with reasonable confidence.

Buffett made this distinction concrete in 2002 when discussing a large finance company. He said: "I understand what they do, but I don't understand everything that's going on within it, and I don't understand that — whether I can continually fund it, you know, on a basis, independent from using Berkshire's credit." [1] He understood every individual transaction the company did, yet he did not regard the whole enterprise as within his circle of competence. [1] That is the gap between product knowledge and business understanding: you can know what a company does and still be unable to judge its sustainability, its funding needs, or its competitive position.

## The cash-flow predictability test

The 1992 letter provides the valuation framework that separates genuine understanding from superficial familiarity. The value of any business is determined by "the cash inflows and outflows — discounted at an appropriate interest rate — that can be expected to occur during the remaining life of the asset." [2] The critical difference between a bond and a stock is that "the investment analyst must himself estimate the future 'coupons.'" [2] If you cannot estimate those future cash flows with enough confidence to justify a purchase price, you do not understand the business.

Buffett describes how Berkshire deals with this: "First, we try to stick to businesses we believe we understand. That means they must be relatively simple and stable in character. If a business is complex or subject to constant change, we're not smart enough to predict future cash flows." [2] Note the condition: simplicity and stability are prerequisites for understanding. A business that is constantly changing may have exciting products, but that does not mean you understand its economics.

## The threshold test, not a risk-adjustment game

In 1998, Buffett explained that he does not use different discount rates to compensate for uncertainty about a business. Instead, he applies a go/no-go threshold: "We look at riskiness, essentially, as being sort of a go/no-go valve in terms of looking at the future businesses. In other words, if we think we simply don't know what's going to happen in the future, that doesn't mean it's necessarily risky, it just means we don't know." [3] He explicitly rejects the idea of saying "we don't know what's going to happen, so therefore we'll discount it at 9 percent instead of 7 percent." [3]

This is a crucial practical distinction. If you find yourself wanting to use a higher discount rate because you are uncertain about the business, you have already answered your own question: you do not understand it well enough. Genuine understanding produces conviction about the range of outcomes, not a vague sense that higher risk requires a higher return.

## The stability and inevitability test

The 1996 letter describes the kind of businesses that are genuinely understandable: those "unlikely to experience major change." [4] Buffett explains that he and Munger search for operations "that we believe are virtually certain to possess enormous competitive strength ten or twenty years from now." [4] A fast-changing industry "may offer the chance for huge wins, but it precludes the certainty we seek." [4]

This is not about predicting quarterly earnings. It is about judging whether a business's competitive position is durable. Buffett uses Coca-Cola as an example: the fundamentals that underlie its competitive dominance and economics "have remained constant through the years," and the reasons people buy the product are "virtually unchanged from what they were in the 1920s." [4] If you cannot identify what makes a business durable for decades, you likely know its products but not its business.

## Knowing the boundary is the competence

Munger made this point sharply in 2002: "if you have competence, you almost automatically have a feeling of where the edge of the competence is. Because after all, it wouldn't be much of a competence if you didn't know its boundary." [1] In 2014, he added that competency is a relative concept and that knowing your limitations is itself a form of wisdom. [5]

Buffett acknowledged that even he has gone outside his circle, particularly in retail. [5] He also noted that his purchase of Berkshire itself was probably outside his circle of competence. [5] The point is not that you will never make mistakes, but that honest self-assessment is the only way to stay within your circle. As Buffett said in 1996: "The size of that circle is not very important; knowing its boundaries, however, is vital." [4]

## Practical self-diagnosis

Based on the sources, here are the questions to ask yourself:

1. **Do I have any doubt?** If yes, you are outside the circle. [1]
2. **Can I estimate future cash flows with reasonable confidence?** If the business is complex or subject to constant change, you cannot. [2]
3. **Am I tempted to use a higher discount rate because I am uncertain?** That is a sign you do not understand the business well enough. [3]
4. **Can I identify why the business will still have strong competitive advantages in ten or twenty years?** If not, you know the product, not the business. [4]
5. **Do I know exactly where my understanding ends?** If you cannot articulate what you do not know, you may not know what you think you know. [1][5]

Product knowledge is a starting point, not a destination. Genuine business understanding produces the confidence to estimate future cash flows, the humility to recognize uncertainty, and the discipline to walk away when doubt remains.

completion.answer:
Reported profit (GAAP net income) differs from the cash an owner can actually take out because GAAP earnings include non-cash charges like depreciation and amortization but **ignore the necessary capital spending and working capital investments required to maintain the business’s competitive position and unit volume**. The owner can only withdraw the cash that remains after those essential reinvestments are made, regardless of what the income statement shows.

### The Owner Earnings Formula

Warren Buffett introduced the concept of "owner earnings" in the 1986 Berkshire letter to bridge exactly this gap. The formula is:

**Owner earnings = (a) reported earnings + (b) depreciation, depletion, amortization, and certain other non-cash charges – (c) the average annual amount of capitalized expenditures for plant and equipment, etc. that the business requires to fully maintain its long-term competitive position and its unit volume.** (If the business also needs additional working capital to maintain its position, that increment is also subtracted in (c).) [1]

The critical insight is that (b) is a non-cash expense added back, but (c) is a real cash outlay that must be subtracted. The owner cannot take (b) home; much of it must stay inside the business just to keep the business from shrinking.

### Why GAAP Can Overstate or Understate Owner Earnings

The 1986 letter illustrates this with the Scott Fetzer acquisition. Before Berkshire bought it, Scott Fetzer’s GAAP net income was $40.2 million. After the purchase, purchase-price accounting adjustments (writing up inventory, fixed assets, and goodwill) caused reported GAAP net income to fall to $28.6 million, even though the underlying economics were identical. Both columns generated the same actual cash for owners. [1]

Buffett explains that for Scott Fetzer, the maintenance capital spending (c) was very close to the old company’s depreciation (b) of $8.3 million. Therefore, owner earnings were far better depicted by the old GAAP earnings of $40.2 million than by the new GAAP figure of $28.6 million. [1]

But the opposite is common. When (c) exceeds (b), GAAP earnings overstate owner earnings. Buffett notes that most managers acknowledge they need to spend more than depreciation over the long term just to hold their ground. The oil industry is a conspicuous example: had major oil companies spent only depreciation each year, they would have guaranteed shrinkage in real terms. [1]

### The "Cash Flow" Fallacy and EBITDA

This is why Buffett calls EBITDA (earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization) "utter nonsense." [3] EBITDA is essentially (a) + (b) without subtracting (c). It implies the business is like the Pyramids—forever state-of-the-art, never needing replacement or refurbishment. [1]

Charlie Munger adds that using EBITDA, a measure known to be nonsense, and then piling additional reasoning on that false assumption, is not a creditable intellectual performance. [3]

The only exception is for businesses with huge initial outlays and tiny ongoing outlays, like a bridge or an extremely long-lived gas field. For manufacturing, retailing, extractive companies, and utilities, (c) is always significant. Over five or ten years, they must make the investment or the business decays. [1]

### How This Affects Valuation

The valuation formula is unchanged since Aesop: you must estimate the amount and timing of cash that will actually emerge from the business and discount it at the risk-free rate (the yield on long-term U.S. bonds). [2] The relevant cash flow is not reported earnings or EBITDA, but the net cash the business can distribute to owners after all necessary reinvestments.

Buffett confirms this approach in 2004: "The business today is worth the present value of all the cash it can distribute between now and Judgment Day." He expects capital expenditures to be, on average, a little more than depreciation unless there is high inflation. [5]

### Practical Distinctions

- **A business that requires little or no capital to grow** (like See’s Candy, which needs only $500,000 to $1 million more than depreciation annually to hold its ground) generates high owner earnings relative to reported earnings. [1]
- **A business that must reinvest all its cash flow just to stay in place** has owner earnings near zero, even if reported profits look healthy.
- **A business that grows but requires heavy capital investment at low returns** can destroy value. Growth is only a plus in the value equation if the discounted cash it generates exceeds the cash inputs required. [2]

The accountants’ job is to record, not to evaluate. The evaluation—estimating (c) and thus true owner earnings—falls to investors and managers. [1]

If the intrinsic value is substantially higher than the price, the shares may be a bargain. The approach is conceptually straightforward but requires disciplined judgment and a clear understanding of the business.

### 1. Define intrinsic value as future distributable cash

Intrinsic value is defined as “the discounted value of the cash that can be taken out of a business during its remaining life” [3]. This is the only logical way to evaluate the relative attractiveness of investments [3]. The cash that can be taken out is not the same as reported earnings; it is the cash the business can distribute to owners after reinvesting enough to maintain its competitive position. In practice, many investors use “look-through earnings” or owner earnings as a rough proxy for distributable cash [2].

### 2. Estimate future cash flows within your circle of competence

You must first decide whether you can sensibly estimate an earnings range for five years out, or more. If you cannot, move on to another prospect [4]. This requires staying inside your **circle of competence** – the set of businesses you truly understand. Buffett advises: “If you have doubts about something being into your circle of competence, it isn’t” [1]. You don’t need to be an expert in every industry, but you must be able to make a rough estimate of the asset’s future earnings [4]. For example, Buffett bought a farm in 1986 after learning from his son how many bushels of corn and soybeans it would produce and what the operating expenses would be; from those estimates he calculated a normalized return of about 10% [4]. He did not need to know everything about farming, only enough to estimate future productivity.

### 3. Apply a discounted cash flow (DCF) framework

The general approach is to project distributable cash over a period (say, 20 years) and then estimate a terminal value, discount all those flows back to the present at an appropriate rate, and sum them to get the business’s intrinsic value [2]. Buffett endorsed this line of thinking when an audience member described it: “The line of thinking is correct, it just depends on what variables you plug in” [2]. The key variables are:

- **Growth assumptions**: How fast can the business grow its distributable cash? Be conservative. Buffett noted that for a large company like Berkshire, growth rates are likely lower than many assume because it becomes harder to deploy capital as the business grows [2].
- **Capital expenditure vs. depreciation**: Expect capital expenditures to be, on average, a little more than depreciation unless there is high inflation [2]. This means owner earnings are typically less than reported earnings.
- **Discount rate**: The rate should reflect the time value of money and the risk of the cash flows. In the 2004 example, the audience used 7% [2]. There is no universal correct rate; it depends on your opportunity cost and the certainty of your estimates.
- **Terminal value**: After the projection period, assume a sustainable level of cash flow (e.g., a perpetual coupon) and discount it back [2].

Reported profit and the cash an owner can actually pull out of a business diverge for two main reasons: some expenses that hit earnings never touch cash, and some cash outlays that keep the business intact never hit earnings. The 1986 owner-earnings appendix lays out the gap as a simple equation, and the Scott Fetzer example makes it concrete.

## The owner-earnings equation

Buffett defines "owner earnings" as (a) reported earnings, plus (b) depreciation, depletion, amortization, and certain other non-cash charges, minus (c) the average annual amount of capitalized expenditures for plant and equipment that the business requires to fully maintain its long-term competitive position and its unit volume. If the business also needs additional working capital to hold that position, that increment belongs in (c) as well, though businesses using LIFO inventory accounting usually do not need extra working capital if unit volume is unchanged [1].

The key point is that (c) is a judgment call, often a hard one, so the result is "vaguely right" rather than "precisely wrong" [1]. Reported GAAP earnings, by contrast, look deceptively precise.

## Non-cash charges that reduce earnings but not cash

When Berkshire bought Scott Fetzer for $315 million against a $172.4 million book value, GAAP required purchase-price adjustments that created four new charges flowing through the income statement: $4,979,000 of non-cash inventory costs, $5,054,000 of extra depreciation from the fixed-asset write-up, $595,000 of goodwill amortization, and $998,000 of deferred-tax adjustments, totaling $11.6 million [1]. None of these are deductible for income tax, so the "new" Scott Fetzer pays exactly the same tax as the "old" one would have, even though GAAP earnings differ sharply [1]. The same sales, wages, and taxes produced identical cash for owners in both columns; only the accounting differed [1].

This is why (b) in the equation is broader than depreciation alone. It includes amortization of intangibles and other purchase-price adjustments, because those are accounting artifacts of an acquisition price, not real economic costs.

## Capital outlays that use cash but not earnings

The other side of the gap is (c). A business that owns factories, stores, or oil wells must keep spending just to stand still. If a company spends only its depreciation each year, it is shrinking in real terms; the oil industry is cited as a conspicuous example [1]. At See's Candies, capitalized expenditures exceed depreciation by $500,000 to $1 million annually simply to hold competitive ground [1]. Munger adds a darker version: some businesses look fine while you keep pouring money in, and then "all of a sudden it doesn't work, and no cash comes back" [3].

Wall Street routinely reports "cash flow" as earnings plus depreciation, without subtracting (c). Buffett calls this "absolute folly" for manufacturing, retailing, extractive companies, and utilities, where reinvestment is always significant [1][3]. EBITDA, in particular, is dismissed as "utter nonsense" because it strips out the cash needed merely to stay in the same place [3]. A business that defers capital spending for a year or two may look cash-rich, but over five or ten years the investment must be made or the business decays [1].

The 1986 appendix shows that owner earnings for the "old" and "new" Scott Fetzer are the same, because (a) plus (b) is the same in both columns and (c) is necessarily the same [1]. You can tell you really understand a business—rather than just knowing its products—when you can confidently answer whether it will still have strong economics in ten or twenty years, and when you have no doubt that it sits inside your circle of competence. If you have any doubt, it does not.

**The core test: doubt means "no"**

Warren Buffett gave a blunt rule in 2002: "if you have doubts about something being into your circle of competence, it isn't." [1] He added that it is "better to be well within the circle than to be trying to tiptoe along the line." [1] So the first test is not positive—it is negative. You do not need to prove you understand a business; you need to check whether you have any doubt. If you do, the answer is no.

Charlie Munger made the same point in 2014: "if you have competence, you almost automatically have a feeling of where the edge of the competence is. Because after all, it wouldn't be much of a competence if you didn't know its boundary." [1] He suggested the question "almost answers itself"—you generally know when you are over your depth, just as you know not to play chess against Bobby Fischer without training. [1]

**Understanding the whole enterprise, not just the transactions**

A key distinction Buffett drew in 2002: understanding what a company does is not the same as understanding the whole enterprise. He described being approached about "a very large finance company":

> "I understand what they do, but I don't understand everything that's going on within it, and I don't understand that—whether I can continually fund it, you know, on a basis, independent from using Berkshire's credit, and so on. So, even though I could understand every individual transaction they did, I don't regard the whole enterprise, or the operation of it, necessarily as being within my circle of competence." [1]

That is a concrete test you can apply to any business: can you understand not just the product and the transactions, but the entire operation—including how it is funded, how it makes money over time, and what could break it? If you can understand every transaction but not the whole enterprise, you do not understand the business.

**The predictability test: will the economics last?**

Buffett's 1996 letter gives the deeper standard. He and Munger favor "businesses and industries unlikely to experience major change" because they are "searching for operations that we believe are virtually certain to possess enormous competitive strength ten or twenty years from now." [4] He contrasted this with fast-changing industries: "A fast-changing industry environment may offer the chance for huge wins, but it precludes the certainty we seek." [4]

He used See's Candies as an example. The company changed in many ways since 1972—different candy assortment, different machinery, different distribution—but "the reasons why people today buy boxed chocolates, and why they buy them from us rather than from someone else, are virtually unchanged from what they were in the 1920s." [4] That is the test: can you identify why customers buy from this company, and can you see that reason persisting for decades?

**What you need to be able to value**

Understanding a business also means being able to estimate its future cash flows. In his 1992 letter, Buffett wrote that the value of any stock, bond, or business is "determined by the cash inflows and outflows—discounted at an appropriate interest rate—that can be expected to occur during the remaining life of the asset." [2] For equities, unlike bonds, "the investment analyst must himself estimate the future 'coupons.'" [2]

He then stated the practical consequence: "we try to stick to businesses we believe we understand. That means they must be relatively simple and stable in character. If a business is complex or subject to constant change, we're not smart enough to predict future cash flows." [2] So a real test of understanding is: can you estimate the future cash flows with reasonable confidence? If you cannot, the business is outside your circle.

**A caution: you can be wrong about your own circle**

Buffett acknowledged in 2014 that even he has gone outside his circle. "I would say that in my own case, I've gone out of it more often in retail than in any other arena. I think it's easy to sort of think you understand retail, and then subsequently find out you don't." [5] He also said buying control of Berkshire Hathaway was likely outside his circle: "That was a dumb decision—which worked out." [5]

This matters for your question because it shows that self-assessment is fallible. Buffett said being "self-realistic" is partly innate—"some people seem a whole lot better at it than the others"—and he noted that some CEOs "have no idea of where their circle of competence begins and ends." [5] He suggested one practical check: "You might get some of your friends that know you well to offer contributions." [5]

**A practical summary**

To tell whether you really understand a business, apply these tests from the sources:

1. **The doubt test**: If you have any doubt about whether the business is in your circle, it is not. [1]
2. **The whole-enterprise test**: Can you understand the entire operation—including funding and long-term viability—not just the individual transactions or products? [1]
3. **The predictability test**: Can you see why customers buy from this company, and can you see that reason persisting for ten to twenty years? [4]
4. **The cash-flow test**: Can you estimate the future cash inflows and outflows with reasonable confidence? If the business is complex or constantly changing, you cannot. [2]
5. **The humility test**: Remember that you can be wrong about your own circle, as Buffett was in retail and with Berkshire itself. [5]

Knowing a company's products is only the beginning. Real understanding means you can see the durable economics, estimate the future cash flows, and have no doubt about the boundary of what you know.

# What Makes Reported Profit Different from Cash an Owner Can Actually Take Out

The core answer, as Warren Buffett explained in the 1986 letter, is that reported (GAAP) earnings include non-cash charges and accounting adjustments that do not reflect actual cash leaving the business, while true owner cash flow must also subtract the capital the business must reinvest just to stay competitive. The two figures can differ substantially.

## The Accounting Distortions

Buffett illustrated this with a 1986 example using Scott Fetzer, a company Berkshire had just acquired. He presented the same business two ways: "Company O" (as if never purchased) and "Company N" (as actually reported after purchase). Both columns show identical economics—same sales, wages, taxes, and same cash generated for owners—but different reported profits: $40.2 million versus $28.6 million [1].

The gap came from purchase-price accounting adjustments. Berkshire paid $315 million for net assets carried at $172.4 million, a $142.6 million premium [1]. Under GAAP, that premium had to be allocated: $37.3 million to inventory, $68.0 million to fixed assets, $13.0 million eliminated from deferred tax liabilities, and the remaining $24.3 million to goodwill [1]. Because the written-up assets must be depreciated or amortized, the "new" company showed higher annual charges to earnings—$4.979 million for non-cash inventory costs, $5.054 million for extra depreciation, $595,000 for goodwill amortization, and $998,000 for deferred-tax adjustments, totaling $11.6 million [1].

Crucially, none of these newly created accounting costs were deductible for income taxes. The "new" Scott Fetzer paid exactly the same tax as the "old" one would have [1]. So the lower reported profit did not mean less cash was available.

## The Owner Earnings Formula

Buffett defined "owner earnings" as:

- (a) reported earnings, plus
- (b) depreciation, depletion, amortization, and certain other non-cash charges, less
- (c) the average annual capitalized expenditures for plant and equipment that the business requires to fully maintain its long-term competitive position and unit volume. If the business needs additional working capital to maintain its position, that increment also belongs in (c) [1].

The key insight: you cannot simply add back all non-cash charges and call the result "cash flow." You must subtract (c), the maintenance capital spending. For Scott Fetzer, Buffett believed (c) was very close to the "old" company's depreciation figure of $8.3 million, and much below the "new" company's $19.9 million of total non-cash charges. Therefore, owner earnings were far better depicted by the "old" column's reported earnings [1].

## Why "Cash Flow" Numbers Mislead

Buffett was sharply critical of the "cash flow" figures routinely presented in Wall Street reports, which add (a) plus (b) but do not subtract (c). These presentations imply the business is "forever state-of-the-art, never needing to be replaced, improved or refurbished" [1]. In manufacturing, retailing, extractive companies, and utilities, (c) is always significant. A business may defer capital spending in a given year, but over five or ten years it must make the investment "or the business decays" [1].

At the 1998 annual meeting, Buffett called EBITDA "utter nonsense" for the same reason: it looks at a figure stated before the cash requirements of merely staying in the same place competitively. Any business with significant fixed assets almost always requires major cash reinvestment just to maintain its position [3]. Charlie Munger added that using a measure known to be nonsense, then piling additional reasoning on that false assumption, is "not creditable intellectual performance" [3].

## The Practical Distinction

The difference between reported profit and distributable cash comes down to three things:

1. **Non-cash accounting charges** (depreciation, amortization, purchase-price adjustments) reduce reported earnings but do not remove cash from the business.
2. **Maintenance capital spending** removes real cash but is not fully captured in depreciation—it must be estimated separately, and it is "a guess—and one sometimes very difficult to make" [1].
3. **Growth capital** is different from maintenance capital. If a business reinvests cash to grow, that cash is not distributable to owners now, but it may generate more cash later. As Buffett said in 1998, a company that reinvests all its cash flow for five years "had better have some very big figures coming in down the road. Because at some day, a financial asset has to give you back cash to justify you laying out cash for it now" [3].

Buffett's conclusion: the accountants' job is "to record, not to evaluate. The evaluation job falls to investors and managers" [1]. Accounting numbers are the starting point, but they are "but an aid to business thinking, never a substitute for it" [1].

He then assumed growth rates of 15% for years one to five and 10% for years six to twenty. [2] Buffett did not endorse those specific numbers—in fact, he said, "I think we might settle for lower numbers on earnings gains than you postulated because we're very large." [2] But he did not quarrel with the general approach of projecting earnings and discounting them. [2]

### 3. Choose a discount rate and handle capital spending

The discount rate is your required return, and it is a variable you must choose. In the 2004 example, the audience member used 7%. [2] Buffett noted, "you're using 7 percent, but the question of what number to use" is open. [2] The sources do not prescribe a specific rate; they treat it as a judgment call.

A critical adjustment involves capital expenditures. The 2004 audience member noted that Berkshire's capital spending exceeded its depreciation by $173 million. [2] Buffett agreed with the caution this implies: "I would say that your assumptions about CAPEX, and related to depreciation, I would expect CAPEX to be, on average, a little more than depreciation unless we run into highly inflationary times." The 2004 exchange is explicit that the inputs are your responsibility: "everybody has to do their own equation and plug in some numbers." observations.question: What makes reported profit different from cash an owner can actually take out of a business?

completion.answer:
## The short answer

Reported profit is an accounting figure; the cash an owner can actually take out is what Buffett calls "owner earnings": reported earnings, plus non-cash charges added back, minus the capital spending the business genuinely needs to stay where it is. The gap between the two comes almost entirely from that last subtraction, which GAAP earnings never make [1].

## The owner-earnings formula

In the 1986 letter appendix, owner earnings are defined as (a) reported earnings, plus (b) depreciation, depletion, amortization and certain other non-cash charges, less (c) the average annual capitalized expenditure the business requires to fully maintain its long-term competitive position and its unit volume. If additional working capital is needed to maintain competitive position and unit volume, that increment is also included in (c) — with the exception that LIFO businesses usually don't need extra working capital if unit volume doesn't change [1].

The key point is that (c) is a guess, and sometimes a very difficult one. But Buffett treats owner earnings, not the GAAP figure, as the relevant number for valuation — for investors buying stocks and managers buying whole businesses — citing Keynes's "I would rather be vaguely right than precisely wrong" [1].

## Why reported profit can mislead

Two distinct problems show up:

**Accounting noise.** Using Scott Fetzer as the example, Buffett shows that purchase-price accounting created $11.6 million of new charges — inventory costs, extra depreciation, goodwill amortization, and deferred-tax adjustments — that were not deductible for tax and reflected no change in the underlying economics. Both versions of the company generated the same cash for owners; only the accounting differed [1]. Owner earnings for the two columns come out identical, because the sum of (a) and (b) is the same and (c) is necessarily the same [1].

**The bigger trap: ignoring (c).** Most managers need to spend more than (b) over the long term just to hold their ground in unit volume and competitive position. When (c) exceeds (b), GAAP earnings overstate owner earnings — frequently substantially, with the oil industry cited as a recent example [1]. This is the absurdity of Wall Street "cash flow" numbers, which add (a) plus (b) but never subtract (c), implying a business is like the Pyramids, never needing replacement or refurbishment. Such shorthand has some utility for businesses making huge initial outlays and tiny outlays thereafter — a bridge or a very long-lived gas field — but it is meaningless for manufacturing, retailing, extractive companies and utilities, where (c) is always significant and deferred spending over a year must be made up over five or ten, or the business decays [1].

At the 1998 meeting, the same point was made about EBITDA: looking at a figure stated before the cash required simply to stay in the same place competitively was called "absolute folly" [3].

## The valuation connection

When valuing a business, the discussion at the 1998 meeting emphasized that a company spending its money as it comes in gets no credit for gross cash flow — only for the net cash left each year — and that a financial asset must eventually deliver cash back to justify cash laid out today [3]. At the 2004 meeting, an audience member's distributable-cash framework was endorsed in general terms, with the caveat that the reply expected capital expenditures to average somewhat more than depreciation (barring highly inflationary times), and that everyone must plug in their own numbers [5].

In short: reported profit is a starting point, but the owner's real cash is what remains after the business pays the full cost of staying in place — and only the owner's judgment about that cost, not the accounting, reveals it.

## The core definition

Start with the definition given in the 1994 letter: intrinsic value is "the discounted value of the cash that can be taken out of a business during its remaining life" [3]. That means a company is worth the present value of all the cash it can distribute between now and, as the 2004 meeting discussion put it, "Judgment Day" [2]. Book value — an easily calculated figure — is described there as "meaningless as an indicator of intrinsic value," useful only as a rough, often understated tracking measure [3]. So the task is not to inspect the balance sheet but to estimate future cash generation and discount it back at an appropriate rate. Any such figure is necessarily highly subjective, changing as cash-flow estimates are revised and as interest rates move [3].

## The practical sequence

The 2013 letter describes how Buffett and Munger actually approach a stock, which they treat as a small portion of a business: first decide whether they can sensibly estimate an earnings range for five years out or more. If yes, they buy only if the price is reasonable relative to the bottom boundary of that estimate. If they cannot estimate future earnings — which they say is usually the case — they simply move on [4]. The same logic appears in the farm example: the analysis focused on what the property would produce (normalized yield, likely productivity gains), not on daily price quotations or macro forecasts [4].

## What the 2004 Berkshire example shows

At the 2004 annual meeting, an audience member walked through a full calculation for Berkshire: starting from operating earnings plus estimated look-through earnings, adjusting for the gap between capital spending and depreciation, projecting growth in two phases, discounting at 7 percent, subtracting liabilities and minority interests, and dividing by the share count [2]. The reply — from the dated meeting discussion, where several turns are unlabeled — endorsed the general line of thinking: estimating distributable cash over time and taking present value is the correct approach, but "it just depends on what variables you plug in," and "everybody has to do their own equation and plug in some numbers" [2]. Two cautions were given: capital expenditure should on average run a little above depreciation (barring highly inflationary times), and earnings-growth assumptions should probably be lower than the questioner postulated, because a very large business finds it harder to deploy incoming capital at high returns [2]. Note that the specific inputs — 15% and 10% growth, a 7% discount rate — were the audience member's assumptions, not prescribed figures, and the 7% rate is a historical example, not a universal discount rate [2].

First, competence. You can only value what you can understand. In the 2002 meeting, Buffett said that if you have doubts about something being in your circle of competence, it isn't — and gave the example of a large finance company where he understood every individual transaction but did not regard the whole enterprise, including whether it could be continually funded independently of Berkshire's credit, as necessarily within his circle [1]. Second, the earnings test itself: if you can't make a rough estimate of an asset's future earnings, the 2013 letter's advice is to forget it and move on [4].

Only after passing both gates does the price question arise — and the bargain judgment is whether the quoted price sits reasonably against the low end of your estimated earnings range [4].
